US.78.es: Brown contra el Consejo de Educación
US.78.def: The landmark 1954 Supreme Court decision that declared state laws establishing separate public schools for Black and white students unconstitutional, overturning Plessy v. Ferguson and ending legal school…

The 12 African American students who integrated Clinton High School in Tennessee in 1956, making it the first state-supported high school in the South to integrate following Brown v. Board of Education.
The nine African American students who integrated Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas in 1957, facing violent mobs and requiring federal troops protection ordered by President Eisenhower.
Chief counsel for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund who argued Brown v. Board of Education before the Supreme Court and later became the first African American Supreme Court Justice in 1967.
Arkansas Governor who defied the Supreme Court by using the National Guard to prevent the Little Rock Nine from integrating Central High School in 1957.
The 1896 Supreme Court case that allowed 'separate but equal' segregation — the precedent overturned by Brown v. Board in 1954.

US.79.def: The "Mother of the Civil Rights Movement" who refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama in 1955, sparking the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
Baptist minister and the most prominent leader of the Civil Rights Movement, advocating nonviolent resistance and delivering the iconic "I Have a Dream" speech at the 1963 March on Washington.
Influential civil rights leader and Nation of Islam minister who advocated for Black nationalism, self-defense, and economic independence before his assassination in 1965.
Birmingham, Alabama's Commissioner of Public Safety who violently opposed civil rights protesters in 1963, using police dogs and fire hoses against peaceful demonstrators, including children.
South Carolina Senator who opposed civil rights legislation and conducted the longest individual filibuster in Senate history (24 hours, 18 minutes) against the Civil Rights Act of 1957.
The strategy of peaceful protest — boycotts, sit-ins, marches — used by Dr. King and others to confront segregation.

US.80.def: The 381-day boycott (1955-1956) of the Montgomery, Alabama bus system by African Americans protesting segregated seating, ending when the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.
Interracial groups of civil rights activists who rode interstate buses into the segregated South in 1961 to challenge illegal segregation of public transportation, facing violent attacks.
Tennessee education center founded in 1932 that trained civil rights leaders including Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr., and John Lewis in nonviolent resistance and organizing tactics.

US.80.es: Ciudad de Tiendas (Condado de Fayette, TN)
US.80.def: A 1960 settlement of African Americans evicted from their homes in Fayette County, Tennessee after registering to vote, living in tents to maintain their right to vote despite economic retaliation.

Nonviolent protests where African Americans sat at segregated lunch counters requesting service, beginning in Greensboro (1960) and powerfully demonstrated in Nashville led by students like Diane Nash.
The massive August 28, 1963 demonstration where over 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to demand civil rights, highlighted by Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech.

US.81.def: Landmark federal legislation that outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, ending segregation in public accommodations and employment.

US.81.es: Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965
US.81.def: Federal legislation that outlawed discriminatory voting practices (literacy tests, poll taxes) used to disenfranchise African Americans, dramatically increasing Black voter registration in the South.

US.81.term: Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Fair Housing Act)
US.81.es: Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1968 (Ley de Vivienda Justa)
US.81.def: Federal law that prohibited discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing based on race, religion, national origin, or sex, addressing residential segregation.
Constitutional amendment ratified in 1964 that abolished poll taxes in federal elections, removing a barrier used to prevent poor African Americans from voting.
The 1963 civil rights rally where Dr. King delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech, pressing for jobs and freedom.
The 36th U.S. President who signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 into law.

US.82.def: Civil rights organization founded in 1968 to address issues of poverty, police brutality, and treaty rights affecting Native Americans, using tactics inspired by the Black civil rights movement.
Mexican American civil rights movement of the 1960s-70s that fought for labor rights, education reform, political representation, and cultural pride, led by figures like Cesar Chavez.
The "Second Wave" women's rights movement that fought for equal pay, reproductive rights, workplace equality, and passage of the Equal Rights Amendment, led by activists like Betty Friedan.
The labor leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers and led nonviolent strikes and boycotts for Mexican American farmworkers.
A proposed constitutional amendment (revived in the 1970s feminist movement) to guarantee equal legal rights regardless of sex.
The labor union founded by Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta to fight for better pay and conditions for farm laborers.
